p: Paul's plural 'brothers' (adelphoi) addresses the whole church, women included.
b: The Greek adelphoi is a masculine plural that Greek used for a mixed group. The site renders it "brothers" everywhere, as in Acts and Romans, and the gloss says "fellow believers, men and women." Paul uses the word about twenty times in this letter, often at a turn in the argument, and here it opens his most careful teaching. He is not giving an order from above but speaking as family. Women prophesy and pray in the Corinthian assembly (11:5), and Paul greets Prisca by name (16:19), so the plural plainly includes them.

a: the good news that I told you
p: Paul uses the noun and the verb together: the good news is something he 'good-newsed' to them.
b: The Greek is euangelion, "good news," and the matching verb euangelizomai, "to announce good news." Paul puts three verbs side by side for the Corinthians' own history with it: they received it, they stand in it, and they are being saved through it. The word "gospel" in older English Bibles is the same Greek word. Paul does not mean a book here. He means the message about Christ's death and rising, which he recites in verses 3 to 5. Notice that he calls it the thing they already know: he is not teaching something new but reminding them of what the resurrection argument rests on.

p: The Greek is a present tense, and the condition that follows is read differently by the churches.
b: Sōzesthe is present tense: "you are being saved," salvation as something under way (compare 1:18, "to us who are being saved"). The condition "if you hold fast" has been read two ways. Traditions that teach that a believer can fall away (Catholic, Orthodox, Wesleyan) take it as a real warning. Traditions that teach that God keeps his people (Reformed) take it as the mark of true faith: those who do not hold fast show they never truly believed. "Unless you believed for no purpose" (eikē, "to no end") fits both: Paul's next verses show what "for no purpose" would mean, a faith in a Christ who was not raised (15:17). See the topic page on perseverance.

t: Of first importance, or first in time?
p: The Greek en prōtois can mean 'first in importance' or 'first in time'; both fit.
b: En prōtois is literally "among the firsts." English Bibles usually say "of first importance," a statement of rank. It can also mean "at the very start," the first things Paul taught when he founded the church in Corinth (Acts 18:1-11). Many commentators hold both senses at once: what he taught first is what matters most. The Plain English Translation's "Among the first things" leaves the choice open. Either way, Paul says that the death and rising of Christ were not a late addition to his message but its base.

a: handed on to you what I also received
t: Received and handed on: a tradition
p: Paul uses the Jewish teacher's words for passing on a fixed teaching.
b: Paradidōmi ("hand on") and paralambanō ("receive") are the Greek words for passing on a teaching, much as later rabbis spoke of receiving and handing on (Hebrew qibbel and masar). Paul uses the pair of the Lord's Supper (11:23) and of this summary. Most scholars, including many who doubt much else in the New Testament, hold that verses 3 to 5 (or 3 to 7) are a short creed Paul learned from the first believers, with signs of a Semitic original: the name Cephas, "the third day," four "that" clauses. If so, it goes back to within a few years of the crucifixion. Paul says where he could have learned it: a visit to Jerusalem to see Cephas (Galatians 1:18-19).

p: The creed says Christ died for sins 'in line with the Scriptures'; Isaiah 53 is the usual background.
b: Paul does not say which Scriptures. The usual suggestion for "died for our sins" is Isaiah 53, where the servant "was pierced because of our rebellions" and "bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:5, 12). Others add the sacrifices of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), Psalm 22, or the whole pattern of the righteous who suffers. The early church gave the suffering Messiah as the sense of "all the Scriptures," as in Luke 24:25-27, 44-46. What the Greek hyper ("for") means exactly, "on behalf of" or "in place of," is the question behind the churches' different teachings on the atonement. See the topic page on atonement.
r: Isaiah 53:5; Isaiah 53:12; Leviticus 16; Luke 24:25; Luke 24:44; Romans 4:25

t: Why burial is in the creed
p: The burial shows the death was real and the tomb was known.
b: A short creed does not waste words. "He was buried" ties the death to a place and a fact: Jesus was laid in a known tomb (Mark 15:46), and the rising that follows is the rising of that body. Preaching in Acts uses the same line (Acts 13:29). Some scholars see in the burial line a hint of the empty tomb, since the creed pairs "was buried" with "has been raised" as two acts on one body. Others stress that Paul never mentions the empty tomb here and rest his case on the appearances. The creed does not settle that, and the Gospels' empty-tomb stories are told in the four Gospels (Mark 16:1-8).

a: has been raised on the third day
p: The perfect tense says he was raised and is still risen; 'third day' follows the Scriptures.
b: Paul writes egēgertai, a perfect passive: "he has been raised," with the result still standing. The passive means it was God's act; the earlier verbs ("died," "was buried") are simple past. "On the third day" counts parts of days as Jewish and Greek counting did. No Old Testament text says "the Messiah will rise on the third day." Hosea 6:2 ("On the third day he will raise us up") is the one most often named; Jonah's three days (Jonah 1:17, used in Matthew 12:40) is another. Later Jewish tradition read "the third day" as a time of rescue in several stories (Genesis Rabbah 56). Paul's point is only that the timing is not an accident: it is "in line with the Scriptures."

p: Cephas is Peter's Aramaic name; the Gospels hint that the Lord appeared to him first.
b: Kēphas is the Aramaic Kepha, "rock," the name Jesus gave Simon (John 1:42), translated into Greek as Petros. Paul prefers the Aramaic form in this letter (1:12; 3:22; 9:5). He lists Cephas first. No Gospel tells the story of that appearance, but Luke's Easter report says the Lord "has appeared to Simon" (Luke 24:34), and Mark 16:7 singles out Peter by name. Paul himself spent fifteen days with Cephas in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:18). Roman Catholic teaching gives Peter's first place a lasting meaning for the church; other traditions read it as the pardon of the man who had denied Jesus. The creed itself only gives the order.

a: more than five hundred brothers at one time
p: No Gospel tells this appearance; only Paul does, and he says many witnesses were alive.
b: This is the only report of the appearance to "more than five hundred." Where it happened is not said. Guesses include the mountain in Galilee of Matthew 28:16-17 (where only the eleven are named) and the day of Pentecost; neither is stated, and Luke's Acts counts only about 120 believers in Jerusalem at the start (Acts 1:15). Paul's remark that "most of them are still alive" is an invitation to ask them, which is how a writer talks who expects to be checked. The word "at one time" (ephapax) says it was a single event, not many small ones. Jewish law counted two or three witnesses as enough (Deuteronomy 19:15); Paul names far more.

p: Sleep is the early Christian word for the death of a believer.
b: Koimaomai is the Greek verb "to sleep" and was used for death in Greek, in the Old Testament ("slept with his fathers") and in the Gospels (Mark 5:39; John 11:11). It became distinctly Christian: the church's burial ground was called a koimētērion, "sleeping place," and our word "cemetery" comes from it. The word does not teach that the soul is unconscious; Paul says elsewhere that to be away from the body is to be with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). It says that death is not final, since sleepers wake. The churches differ on what happens between death and the resurrection; see the card at 15:35-54.

p: James is Jesus' brother, who led the Jerusalem church; his appearance is known only from Paul.
b: This is James the brother of Jesus, whom Paul met in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19) and who led the church there (Acts 15:13; 21:18). His brothers did not believe in Jesus during his life (John 7:5), so an appearance to James would explain the change. The Gospels do not tell it. Jerome, in Lives of Illustrious Men (the entry on James), quotes a story from the Gospel of the Hebrews that James had sworn not to eat until he saw the Lord risen, and that Jesus appeared to him; the Gospel of the Hebrews is lost and survives only in quotations.

t: 'All the apostles': a wider group than the Twelve
p: Paul separates the Twelve from a larger circle of apostles, sent ones.
b: "The Twelve" (verse 5) was the group Jesus chose. "All the apostles" is a wider group, which in Paul's letters includes Barnabas (1 Corinthians 9:5-6), Andronicus and Junia (Romans 16:7), and Paul himself. The word apostolos means "one sent." Paul's own claim to the title rests on this very verse and the next: he saw the risen Lord (9:1) and was sent. The Corinthians were being asked to measure Paul against others (1:12; 9:1-3), so the list ends with him on purpose. The word "all" shows the circle was large and closed: appearances "last of all" came to Paul.

a: as to one born at the wrong time
p: Ektrōma is a miscarried or stillborn child; Paul's meaning is debated.
b: Ektrōma names a child born dead or too early. The Greek Old Testament uses it of a stillborn child (Numbers 12:12; Job 3:16 speaks of a hidden miscarriage). Three readings are common. (1) Paul was late, born into the apostolic circle after the rest, as if born at the wrong time. (2) It is an insult his critics threw at him (ugly, unformed, not a real apostle) and he takes it up humbly. (3) It speaks of his unfitness, a monster that should not have lived, saved only by grace; Ignatius of Antioch later wrote of himself, in his letter to the Roman church (chapter 9), as one who was born out of due time, echoing this verse. The Plain English Translation follows the oldest English sense, "born out of time."

a: I persecuted the church of God
p: Paul never hides that he hunted believers; it is part of why grace is his theme.
b: Paul tells the same fact in Galatians 1:13 and Philippians 3:6, and Acts shows him approving Stephen's death and arresting believers (Acts 8:3; 9:1-2). He does not say it for sympathy. It sets up verse 10: the one least fit is the one grace made. Here "the church of God" is the whole movement, not only the Corinthians. His past is also a witness for the Corinthians, because a persecutor changed by meeting the risen Lord is the strongest proof he can offer that the appearances happened.

a: I toiled more than all of them
p: Paul works hard and says it was grace; churches have read the balance differently.
b: Two words matter. Kopiaō, "toil," is hard labor, the word he uses of his own work and of the labor of those he honors (16:16). And charis, "grace," is his main word for God's undeserved gift. The sentence refuses both of two mistakes: it is not that Paul did nothing, and it is not that he earned it. "Not I, but the grace of God that is with me" is read in the Catholic and Orthodox traditions as grace working together with a free will (the Greek syn, "with"), and in the Reformed tradition as grace doing all and the labor as its fruit. Both quote this verse. A small textual question touches the phrase (whether the article stands before "with me"); it does not remove the word syn from either reading (see the variant note). The churches' cards on grace and works sit at Romans 3 to 5 and Ephesians 2.
orig: ἡ χάρις ... ἡ σὺν ἐμοί (hē charis ... hē syn emoi)

t: Who in Corinth denied the resurrection?
p: Paul does not say what the 'some' believed; scholars offer several views.
b: Paul says only that some "say no resurrection of the dead exists." Views: (1) Greek thinkers hoped for the soul's survival but thought a raised body absurd (Aeschylus has Apollo say that once a man's blood is spilled there is "no resurrection," Eumenides 647-648; Athens laughed at Paul on this, Acts 17:32). (2) Some held, like Epicureans, that death ends everything. (3) Some held that the resurrection had already happened spiritually, as Hymenaeus and Philetus did later (2 Timothy 2:18); Paul's mocking "already you are kings" in 4:8 fits this. (4) Some denied a bodily rising yet believed in the Lord's. Commentators weigh these; Paul's answer ("what sort of body," verses 35-49) suits views 1 and 4 best.

a: no resurrection of the dead exists
t: The resurrection hope Paul shared with Pharisees
p: Paul argues from a Jewish hope the Pharisees held and the Sadducees denied.
b: The hope that God will raise the dead is clearest in Daniel 12:2: "Many of those asleep in the dusty ground will wake up." By the first century the Pharisees held it and the Sadducees denied it (Acts 23:8). The Mishnah later says that anyone who denies that the resurrection of the dead is taught in the Torah has no share in the world to come (Sanhedrin 10:1), and the second blessing of the daily Jewish prayer, the Amidah, praises God "who gives life to the dead." Paul writes as a Pharisee-trained Jew (Philippians 3:5; Acts 23:6). The Corinthian Gentiles lacked this background. For Paul the resurrection is a general hope that Christ's rising has already begun.

p: The Greek preposition kata can mean 'against'; a false claim about what God did is a charge against him.
b: Kata with a genitive often means "against," and "testified against God" is a possible sense: to claim that God raised someone he did not raise would be a lie told in his name. Most translations soften it to "about," and the Plain English Translation does too. Paul's logic is sharp. He is not asking the Corinthians to value resurrection as a pleasant idea. He says that if there is no rising of the dead, then the apostles' central testimony is false, and false in the courtroom sense (pseudomartyres, "false witnesses"). Deuteronomy 19:15-19 treats a false witness as a serious wrong; Paul will not claim to be innocent of it if Christ was not raised.
orig: ψευδομάρτυρες ... κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ (pseudomartyres ... kata tou theou)

a: you are still in your sins
p: Paul ties the forgiveness of sins to the resurrection, not only to the cross.
b: Verse 3 said "Christ died for our sins." Here Paul adds that if he was not raised, the Corinthians are "still in your sins." So the death by itself does not finish the work in Paul's mind; the rising is God's vindication of it. Romans 4:25 says the same in a pair: Jesus was handed over for our offenses and raised for our justification. The churches handle this differently in teaching, some placing weight on the cross and others on the whole Easter event (the Orthodox sing of Christ trampling death by death). Paul himself keeps them together, and the Corinthians' denial would break them apart.
orig: ἔτι ἐστὲ ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν (eti este en tais hamartiais hymōn)

p: The first ripe grain, offered to God, promised the rest of the harvest.
b: Under the law, Israel brought "a sheaf from the first of your harvest" to the priest before anyone ate of the new grain (Leviticus 23:10). The sheaf was waved "the day after the Sabbath" (Leviticus 23:11) in the week of Passover, and the Jewish festival of Weeks, fifty days on, closed the grain harvest (Deuteronomy 16:9-10). The firstfruits was not a separate crop; it was the first of the same crop, and its presentation made the whole harvest ready. So Christ is the first of the resurrection of the dead, and the rest are the same kind, not a different one. Paul has already called the Passover lamb Christ (5:7).
r: Leviticus 23:10; Leviticus 23:11; Deuteronomy 16:9; 1 Corinthians 5:7; Romans 8:23; Colossians 1:18

t: Adam in 1 Corinthians and in Romans
p: Adam stands for the human family under death; Paul draws the same pair in Romans 5.
b: Paul does not argue for Adam's historical existence here or tell how death passed on. He takes the figure from Genesis 2 to 3: the man of dust who ends up returning to dust (Genesis 3:19: "to dust you will go back"). "In Adam" and "in Christ" name two groups or two realms of life people belong to. Romans 5:12-21 sets out the same pair at length, and the churches disagree about it (original sin; see the card at Romans 5). Whether Adam was one man, a type for all humanity, or both is argued among Christians and Jews alike.

a: all will be made alive in Christ
p: Does 'all' mean everyone, or all who belong to Christ? Verse 23 narrows it, say some.
b: The first "all" (die in Adam) is everyone. Does the second "all" match it? (1) All who are in Christ. Verse 23 says "those who belong to Christ." Most Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and evangelical readers take it this way; "made alive" means raised to life with Christ. (2) Everyone is raised, but not all to blessing. Some hold that the verse is about the resurrection itself, which Jesus says includes some to judgment (John 5:28-29; Daniel 12:2). (3) Everyone will be saved. Origen and Gregory of Nyssa have been read this way, building on 15:28; the church later condemned a form of Origen's teaching, and the churches still debate how far Gregory went. The card below sets churches side by side.

a: its own place in the order
t: Tagma: a rank in the line
p: The Greek tagma is a military word: a unit with its place in the line.
b: Tagma is used for a rank, division or unit of an army. Paul's picture: the risen dead come in a sequence, as a parade moves by units. First Christ, "the firstfruits," and then, "at his coming" (parousia), those who belong to him. The early letter 1 Clement uses the same army picture when it says that each one does what he is told "in his own rank" (1 Clement 37). Notice what the list lacks: Paul does not describe a third group or a long gap. He reads the rising of the believers as coming straight after the appearing of Christ, which is why the next verse's "then" matters to those who read in millennium views.

t: 'Then' and 'the end': does a millennium fit?
p: Paul's 'then comes the end' is read by some as a gap and by others as no gap.
b: Eita to telos is literally "then the end." Eita means "next" or "after that" and does not say how long. Premillennialists such as George Ladd read Christ's coming (verse 23), a reign, and then the end (verses 24-28) as the same order that Revelation 20 gives; the reign Paul speaks of in verse 25 is, on this reading, the thousand years. Amillennialists read the rule of Christ in verse 25 as his present reign from the right hand of God (Psalm 110:1), and "the end" as coming at his return. Postmillennial and others differ again. Paul says nothing here of a thousand years, so each reading brings it to the text.

a: every rule and every authority and power
p: Paul's list names spiritual forces and human rulers together.
b: Archē, exousia and dynamis ("rule," "authority," "power") are words Paul uses for the powers that stand behind the world's order, some human, some spiritual (Romans 8:38; Ephesians 1:21; 6:12; Colossians 2:15). Earlier, Paul spoke of the "rulers of this age" who crucified the Lord of glory (2:8). Most scholars today think he means unseen powers as well as earthly governments, since the sequence ends with death as the last "enemy." What is worth noticing is the verb katargeō, "bring to an end" or "make powerless": it does not say these are destroyed in the sense of ceasing to exist, only that they lose their hold.

a: he places all the enemies under his feet
p: Paul's phrase is Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes most.
b: The psalm says: "The LORD declares to my lord: 'Sit at my right hand, until I set your enemies down as a stool for your feet.'" Jesus used it in debate (Mark 12:35-37), and Acts, Hebrews and the letters rely on it. The Hebrew "my lord" (adoni) was read as the king, and later by some Jews as the Messiah. Paul uses "until" to say that Christ's rule is now ongoing and has a goal. Note that in the psalm the LORD puts the enemies down; Paul's verse leaves unclear whether the "he" who places them is Christ or God, and verse 27 will say the Father did it.

p: Paul speaks of death as a hostile power, the last one to fall.
b: Many Greeks saw death as natural, even a friend that freed the soul. Paul calls it an enemy (echthros). In Genesis death comes as the result of the man's disobedience (Genesis 3:19), and in Romans it "reigned" (Romans 5:14, 17). The Old Testament pictures God one day swallowing death (Isaiah 25:8, quoted in 1 Corinthians 15:54). "Last" is in order: the others (rule, authority, power) go first, and death goes last. Revelation 20:14 has death thrown into the lake of fire. For Paul this makes the resurrection of the body more than a comfort for the soul: it is the defeat of an enemy.

a: he put all things under his feet
p: Paul applies a psalm about humans to Christ; Hebrews 2 does the same.
b: Psalm 8 praises God that he made humankind rulers over his works: "everything you have placed beneath his feet" (Psalm 8:6). That is Adam's calling in Genesis 1:26-28. Paul quotes it in the Greek form ("he put all things under his feet") and reads it of Christ as the true human, the last Adam (15:45). Hebrews 2:6-9 makes the same move at more length. The thought joins Adam and Psalm 110 here: the one who completes the human task is the one the Father rules through. Paul then adds a careful exception: the One who put all things under him is not himself included.

a: the Son himself will also be put under the One
t: The Son put under the Father
p: Paul says the Son will be 'put under' God; the churches read this differently.
b: The verb hypotagēsetai is passive: "will be put under." It might also be read as middle, "will put himself under." Churches that confess one God in three equal persons (Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and most others) say it speaks of the Son's role as mediator and as the human Lord: he gives the kingdom back, the work done. Augustine and Calvin both read it that way. Groups that teach the Son is a lesser being (Jehovah's Witnesses, Unitarians) read it as the Son's subordination by nature. The creed of Constantinople (381) says of Christ, "his kingdom will have no end." The card below gives each church's answer.

a: so that God may be all in all
p: The phrase says God will be everything to everyone, and it can be read in several ways.
b: Ho theos ta panta en pasin is literally "the God the all in all." It can mean that God will be everything in everything, God's rule fully real throughout creation, or that God will be everything to every person. Origen used it to hope that every creature would at last be restored to God (On First Principles 3.6); the church condemned that in later centuries, and the mainstream read it as the end of all resistance. Greek philosophers also spoke of a God who is "all," and Paul is not saying that God and the world are the same thing. Compare Ephesians 4:6 and Colossians 3:11.
orig: ὁ θεὸς τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν (ho theos ta panta en pasin)

p: The most puzzling verse in the letter: dozens of explanations, none certain.
b: Paul speaks of "those who are baptized for the dead" without approving or condemning it, and uses it only as an argument. Main readings: (1) Proxy baptism: living believers were baptized in place of friends or relatives who had died unbaptized. Chrysostom (Homilies on 1 Corinthians 40) says the Marcionites did this for dead catechumens, and also reads the baptism as a sign of the resurrection of the body; Epiphanius (Panarion 28.6) says the Cerinthians did it. Both wrote about groups later than Paul (Marcion lived long after this letter), so they cannot show what Paul meant. Tertullian names no group: in Against Marcion 5.10 he says Paul mentions the practice only to press the resurrection of the body and takes "baptized for the dead" to mean baptized for the body; in On the Resurrection of the Flesh 48 he says those who practiced vicarious baptism did so in the belief of a bodily resurrection, and uses that in the same way. Many modern scholars read it as vicarious baptism that Paul neither approves nor condemns. (2) Baptism in hope of rejoining dead believers. (3) A picture of dying with Christ. (4) A local custom (DeMaris reads it against the religion of Corinth, using archaeology and anthropology). The card below shows how the churches treat it.
orig: βαπτιζόμενοι ὑπὲρ τῶν νεκρῶν (baptizomenoi hyper tōn nekrōn)

p: Paul's hardships in Ephesus and Asia give the 'danger' a real meaning.
b: Paul lists his dangers elsewhere: beatings, shipwreck, plots (2 Corinthians 11:23-27; Acts 19:23-41). His stay in Ephesus brought a riot over the goddess Artemis and, he says in 2 Corinthians 1:8-10, trouble in Asia so heavy that he despaired of life. The point for the argument is a question of motive: if the dead are not raised, then a life of constant risk is a poor bargain. The sentence is aimed at Paul's critics in Corinth who judged him by comfort and status (4:8-13): he suffers because he stakes his life on the very rising they doubt.

p: Paul does not mean he is literally dead; he is describing a life always close to death.
b: The Greek kath' hēmeran apothnēskō is a present tense: "daily I am dying." Another letter says he always carries in his body the dying of Jesus (2 Corinthians 4:10-11). Paul's version is not a method; it is his report that apostleship exposes him to death. The oath that follows, "by the pride I have in you," is unusual: he swears by the Corinthians as his boast before God, to show how real his words are.

a: fought with wild beasts at Ephesus
p: Did Paul fight actual animals in the arena, or does he describe human enemies?
b: Ethēriomachēsa can mean literally to fight wild animals as a condemned man. That is rare for a Roman citizen like Paul (Acts 22:25-29), and he does not list it among the dangers in 2 Corinthians 11. Most scholars take it as figurative: opponents in Ephesus called "beasts," a use found in Greek writers, and Ignatius of Antioch later wrote of his own fight with beasts on the way to Rome (Romans 5). A few ancient and modern readers take it literally, because Paul adds "as a mere man." The phrase "as a mere man" (kata anthrōpon) is also debated: "to speak humanly" or "with human aims." Acts 19 describes the Ephesian riot but not an arena.

p: Paul quotes the slogan of people who give up on God; Isaiah quoted it first.
b: In Isaiah 22:12-13 the LORD called Jerusalem to mourn, but the people held a feast instead: "Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!" Paul uses the Septuagint's wording. The slogan was also popular in Greek life: Herodotus (Histories 2.78) says the Egyptians showed a corpse at banquets with a call to drink. Wisdom of Solomon 2:1-9 puts almost the same thoughts in the mouth of the ungodly who see life as short. Paul offers the other side of the choice: if death is the end, this is the sane answer; because it is not the end, it is not.
r: Isaiah 22:13; Isaiah 22:12; Wisdom of Solomon 2:6; Luke 12:19

t: A line from a Greek comedy
p: Paul quotes a proverb ancient writers credit to the poet Menander.
b: "Bad company ruins good habits" is a verse in Greek comic meter (an iambic line) that is commonly traced to the Athenian comic playwright Menander and his play Thaïs; it had become a proverb. The church historian Socrates Scholasticus (Church History 3.16) says instead that Paul knew the saying from the tragedies of Euripides. Paul uses it as a warning that the Corinthian doubters' company is changing the church's habits. He quotes Greek poets elsewhere only rarely (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12). The word "habits" (ēthē) gives us "ethics." There is no suggestion that Menander's play is endorsed. It is an example of Paul turning a common saying into a pastoral point, as he does with the Corinthians' own slogans in 6:12 and 8:1.
orig: φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί (phtheirousin ēthē chrēsta homiliai kakai)

a: what sort of body do they come in
p: 'How?' and 'with what body?' are the questions of someone who finds a raised body absurd.
b: Paul voices an objector ("someone will say"), as in a diatribe, the lively teaching style of Greek schools (Romans 2 and 3 use it too). The first question is about how the dead can be raised, the second about what kind of body they would have. A common Greek view was that the body is the soul's prison and its end is a release. Another worry: if a body decays, where do its parts go? Jewish writers faced the same puzzle (2 Baruch 49:2-3 asks with what form the raised will live). Paul does not answer with a lecture on biology. He answers with seeds, stars and two Adams.

p: The sower's picture was familiar; Jesus used it too.
b: "Fool!" (aphrōn) is a sharp word for someone who should know better; Paul uses it again in 2 Corinthians 11 and Jesus uses a related word in Luke 12:20. The picture of a seed that must "die" to live was common in the farming world. Jesus used the same image of his own death: "if a grain of wheat does not fall into the earth and die, it remains a single grain. But if it dies, it produces a lot of fruit" (John 12:24). Paul's "you yourself" is emphatic: the objector sows every year. The point is not that the seed is a proof of resurrection, but that life from apparent death is part of everyday creation.

p: Paul stresses both continuity (a body) and change (God gives it a new form).
b: Two truths sit together. First: God gives a body, so the future life is not bodiless. Second: the grain that is sown is not the plant that rises. Readers have weighed these differently. Irenaeus and Tertullian stress that it is the flesh that rises (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.9; Tertullian, On the Resurrection of the Flesh). Modern scholars such as N. T. Wright and Dale Martin differ in turn on how "physical" Paul's "spiritual body" is. The Plain English Translation uses the literal "body," leaving that to the notes.

a: Not every kind of flesh is the same
t: The ancient map of living things
p: Paul lists humans, animals, birds and fish, as Genesis does.
b: The four kinds echo the creation account, where God makes sea creatures and birds, then land animals, then humankind (Genesis 1:20-27). Ancient people grouped living things this way, and Paul's point is that God has made many kinds of bodies, each fitted to its place: land, air, water. If God can make flesh of such different kinds, then he can make a body suited to the age to come. The argument is by analogy, not proof. Paul stops at what the creator can do and moves to the heavens.

p: The sun, moon and stars are named in verse 41, but some hear angels.
b: Most commentators take "heavenly bodies" as the sun, moon and stars Paul names in the next verse. Ancient people often thought the stars were living beings (Job 38:7 pairs the morning stars with the "sons of God"), so some think Paul may include angelic beings. "Glory" (doxa) then means brightness. The idea that the raised will shine is in Daniel 12:3: "will blaze like the stars, for ever and ever." Later movements have used verses 40 to 42 for "degrees of glory" in the afterlife; the Latter-day Saints cite the sun, moon and stars for their three kingdoms of glory (Doctrine and Covenants 76). Most other churches do not read it so, and see in it only the difference in glory between this body and the next.

p: Paul's 'sown' may picture a burial, or the whole of mortal life.
b: The six contrasts of verses 42 to 44 all have the same grammar: it is sown in one condition and raised in another. Most commentators take "sown" as burial, a corpse put in the ground like a seed (as in John 12:24). Some Fathers and later readers took it as the whole mortal life from birth. In both readings the "it" is the same: the person, not a different thing. "Decay" and "cannot decay" (phthora, aphtharsia) belong to the language of Greek thought about perishing, and "dishonor" and "weakness" are the marks of a dead body. Each contrast ends in a gain: glory and power.

p: Psychikos comes from psyche, 'soul' or 'life'; it means a body animated by ordinary life.
b: Psychikos is built on psychē, "soul" or "life-breath." It describes a person or body driven by the ordinary life God gave Adam, the life of the living being (verse 45). Paul used the same adjective for the "natural person" who does not accept the things of the Spirit (2:14). English "natural" is the usual choice, but it can mislead: "soulish" is closer, and some translations say "physical." The contrast is not between body and soul. It is between a body ruled by the soul's life as it now is and a body ruled by God's Spirit. See also Jude 19.

p: A body made of spirit, or a body ruled by the Spirit? The churches mostly say the second.
b: Greek -ikos endings say what a thing is animated or governed by, not what it is made of: a "spiritual person" (2:15) is a person led by the Spirit, not a ghost. So most Fathers and nearly all modern commentators read "spiritual body" as a real body transformed and governed by the Spirit. Some scholars note that Stoics thought spirit (pneuma) was a fine kind of matter, and Troels Engberg-Pedersen argues that Paul meant a body made of such stuff; most reply that Paul's Spirit is God's Spirit. Groups that teach that Jesus rose as a spirit (Jehovah's Witnesses) read it differently again; the Gospels' Jesus eats fish and shows his wounds (Luke 24:39-43). The card at the end of this section sets the churches side by side.

p: Paul quotes Genesis 2:7 and adds 'first' and 'Adam' to set up the second Adam.
b: The Greek Old Testament of Genesis 2:7 reads: "the man became a living soul." This site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "the man became a living being" (Genesis 2:7). Paul adds two words that Genesis does not have, "first" and "Adam," so the verse can answer the new phrase "the last Adam." The Greek psychē ("soul, being") links to the adjective psychikos in verse 44. In Hebrew, nephesh chayyah is also used of animals (Genesis 1:20); Paul's reading gives it to Adam as the typical earthly man. Christ becomes the true human, the beginning of a new humanity.

t: The last Adam as life-giving spirit
p: Does Paul identify Christ with the Spirit, or say what Christ does through the Spirit?
b: "Life-giving" (zōopoioun) is the work of God (John 5:21; Romans 4:17). Paul says Christ became "a spirit that gives life," and 2 Corinthians 3:17 says "the Lord is the Spirit." Trinitarian churches read these lines as describing what the risen Christ does by the Spirit, not as a claim that the Son and the Spirit are one person. Philo of Alexandria had two creations of the human: a heavenly man (Genesis 1:27) first and an earthly man (Genesis 2:7) after (On the Creation). Paul reverses it (verse 46): the earthly first, the heavenly last.

p: Does 'from heaven' mean Christ came from heaven, or that his rising is of heaven's kind?
b: The Greek ex ouranou ("out of heaven") sets Christ's origin against Adam's "out of earth." Some read it as Christ's pre-existence (he came down); others read it as the origin of his resurrection life, since the whole passage is about the future body. Paul's line on the future is in verse 49. The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus add "the Lord" ("the second man is the Lord from heaven"), which is the KJV reading; see the variant note.

a: worn the image of the one made of dust
t: Image of Adam, image of Christ
p: The image language comes from Genesis 1:26-27 and 5:3.
b: In Genesis God makes the human "in his image" (Genesis 1:27), and later Adam fathers a son "in his likeness, by his image" (Genesis 5:3). Paul reads the second text: all of Adam's descendants carry Adam's image, mortality included. In the new creation they will carry Christ's. Elsewhere Paul says believers are being changed into Christ's image (2 Corinthians 3:18; Romans 8:29) and that the body of lowliness will be made like his body of glory (Philippians 3:21). The verb phoreō means to wear or carry as clothing or a burden. A textual variant gives "let us wear" instead of "we will wear"; see the variant entry.

a: flesh and blood is not able to inherit the kingdom of God
t: 'Flesh and blood' does not mean 'no bodies'
p: Some read this as 'the body will not be raised'; the phrase means mortal human nature.
b: "Flesh and blood" is a Jewish phrase for ordinary, mortal human beings (Sirach 14:18; Matthew 16:17; Galatians 1:16; Hebrews 2:14). The verse's second half explains it: "Decay does not inherit what cannot decay." The point is that mortal life, as it is, cannot enter God's kingdom without change. Some have used the verse against a physical resurrection (and Irenaeus fought that use in Against Heresies 5.9-10, arguing that flesh is exactly what God saves). Others, and the teaching of Jehovah's Witnesses, read it to mean the raised body is not made of flesh. Paul's next lines ("we will be changed") say the change happens to the same people.

p: In Paul, a mystery is a secret of God now made known, not a puzzle.
b: Mystērion is something hidden that God has now revealed (2:7; Romans 11:25; 16:25). Here the revealed secret is that not everyone will die before the end, and that those alive will be changed with the dead. In 1 Thessalonians 4:15-17 Paul writes the same event, with "we who are alive" among those who will meet the Lord. The Jewish apocalypses speak of secrets revealed to seers (Daniel 2:28-30; 4 Ezra 14). Paul says "we" will be changed, and some conclude he expected to be alive at the return; others note that he also reckoned with dying first (2 Corinthians 5:1-8; Philippians 1:21-23).

p: The ram's horn blast marks God's decisive day in the Old Testament and in Jewish prayer.
b: In Isaiah 27:13 "a great ram's horn will be blown" and the scattered come home. The prophets use the trumpet for the day of the LORD (Joel 2:1; Zephaniah 1:16), and at Sinai a trumpet sounded as God came down (Exodus 19:16). Jesus speaks of angels sent "with a great trumpet" to gather the chosen (Matthew 24:31), and 1 Thessalonians 4:16 has "the trumpet of God." Some Jewish readers link the horn with Rosh Hashanah, the New Year, which the Jewish tradition calls a day of judgment; Paul does not make that link. Some Christians have tied this "last" trumpet to the seventh trumpet in Revelation 11:15, others to the end-time horn of Jewish prophecy.

a: Death has been swallowed up in victory
p: Paul quotes Isaiah 25:8 in a form that differs from both the Hebrew and the Septuagint.
b: This site's Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "He will swallow death up for all time" (Isaiah 25:8). The Hebrew lanetsach ("for all time") can also carry the sense "to victory" in Aramaic and later Hebrew. The standard Greek Old Testament reads "Death has swallowed up [or prevailed over] ..." but the later Greek translation of Theodotion reads "Death was swallowed up in victory," the form Paul uses. Paul may be using an older Greek version or translating himself. Revelation 21:4 finishes the picture with the tears wiped away, the next line of Isaiah 25:8.
orig: κατεπόθη ὁ θάνατος εἰς νῖκος (katepothē ho thanatos eis nikos)

p: Paul takes Hosea's call for death's plagues and turns it into a song of triumph.
b: In Hosea God asks: "Where are your plagues, Death? Where is your destruction, Sheol?" (Hosea 13:14). In context it may be a threat, calling death to come against Ephraim. The Greek translation already reads "Where is your penalty (dikē), Death? Where is your sting (kentron), Hades?" Paul keeps "sting," changes "penalty" to "victory," and puts "Death" in both lines, so that the believer mocks Death after the resurrection. The Textus Receptus and Byzantine text bring "Hades" back into the second line, which is the KJV reading ("O grave"); see the variant entry. Death's "sting" is the stinger of a scorpion or bee. The shift from threat to triumph is how the New Testament often uses the prophets.

a: the power of sin is the law
p: Paul says the Torah gives sin its force; he does not call the Torah bad.
b: The line is compressed. Elsewhere Paul explains it: the law shows what sin is and gives sin an opening (Romans 7:7-13), and where there is a command, breaking it brings death (Romans 4:15; 5:13). The same Paul says the law is holy and good (Romans 7:12). Jewish readers ask whether "the law" here is the Torah as given to Israel or a general principle of command. Because 15:56 reads like a comment on the quotation, a few scholars have called it a later gloss; no manuscript omits it. Verse 57 turns at once to thanks.

t: Why the resurrection makes work matter
p: The chapter ends with work: the labor done 'in the Lord' lasts.
b: Paul's "so then" brings the whole argument to a plain demand. Because the dead will be raised, nothing done in the Lord is lost. The word "toil" (kopos) is the same as in 15:10 and 16:16, and "empty" (kenos) repeats the word that governed verses 10 and 14. The end of a long doctrinal argument is not speculation about the next age but "the work of the Lord" now. The resurrection is thus the ground of the church's daily work in the world, not an escape from it. Compare Revelation 14:13, where the deeds of those who die in the Lord follow them.
orig: κόπος οὐκ ἔστιν κενός (kopos ouk estin kenos)

p: A fund among Paul's churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem; it runs through his letters.
b: Logeia ("collection") is a word found in Greek papyri for money gathered for a god or temple, and Paul uses it for this fund. "The saints" here means the believers in Jerusalem (compare Romans 15:25-26). The Jerusalem church was poor: a famine under Claudius had struck (Acts 11:28-30), and at the meeting in Jerusalem Paul had been asked to "remember the poor," which he was eager to do (Galatians 2:10). Scholars give several purposes: simple relief, a sign of unity between Gentile and Jewish believers, and the nations bringing gifts to Zion as the prophets had said (Isaiah 60:5-7; Romans 15:16). The letter 2 Corinthians 8-9 later treats it at length. Paul carried it to Jerusalem in the end (Acts 24:17).

p: Paul says he gave the Galatian churches the same orders; this letter shows they were part of it.
b: The "churches of Galatia" are the congregations Paul founded in the Roman province in what is now central Turkey (Acts 16:6; 18:23), the same churches addressed in his letter to the Galatians. We have no letter of his that gives the order Paul mentions, so the instruction was given orally or in a lost letter. The order shows how Paul ran the project: one plan across his churches, each doing its part, so that Jerusalem would see the whole Gentile mission give together. Later, Acts lists the delegates who traveled with the money, naming men from Asia, Macedonia and Galatia (Acts 20:4).

a: On the first day of the week
t: The first day of the week
p: A Jewish way to say 'Sunday'; the earliest hint that Christians gathered on that day.
b: The Greek kata mian sabbatou is literally "according to one of the Sabbath," the Jewish way to name the first day of the seven. Jewish speech had no names for the weekdays other than the Sabbath. The first day was the day of the Lord's rising (John 20:1, 19), and Acts 20:7 says the believers in Troas gathered "to break bread" on that day. Revelation 1:10 calls it "the Lord's day." Later writers confirm the pattern: the Didache says to gather on the Lord's day (14:1), and Justin Martyr's description of Sunday worship includes a collection for the needy (First Apology 67). Whether Paul here assumes a Sunday gathering, or only a convenient weekly date, is debated.

p: The Greek para heautō is 'by himself': saving privately at home, or setting it apart in the gathering?
b: Par' heautō means "beside himself," that is, "at his own place." Most read it as each person saving at home (the Plain English Translation's reading), so that the money would be ready when Paul came and no collection would need to be made under pressure. A few readers take it as "with the community" or as the believer putting it aside in the church's chest, since Justin shows a weekly collection in the assembly. "Whatever he has had success earning" has been read as giving in proportion to earnings. It does not set a percentage; the tithe of the law (10%) is not mentioned, and 2 Corinthians 8:12 says that giving is measured by what a person has. See the card at this verse.

p: Paul lets the Corinthians choose their own delegates and sends letters so no one can doubt them.
b: To approve (dokimazō) is to test and accept. The Greek is ambiguous: "whoever you approve, I will send with letters" (Paul writes the letters), or "whoever you approve with letters" (the church writes letters). Either way, the church chooses the carriers, as Paul explains in 2 Corinthians 8:18-21: he wants to avoid any charge that he handled the money for himself. In the ancient world, travelers with letters of recommendation were the norm (Romans 16:1-2). Paul's care for accountability still reads as a model. Acts 20:4 names the later delegates; Corinth's carriers are not named there.

t: Paul's route and later change of plans
p: Paul meant to cross Macedonia and then spend time at Corinth; he later changed the plan.
b: Macedonia, the Roman province north of Achaia, held Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea, where Paul had founded churches (Acts 16 to 17). The sea route from Ephesus to Corinth was shorter. Paul planned to go the long way, by land through Macedonia, perhaps to gather the Macedonian share of the collection (2 Corinthians 8:1-5). In 2 Corinthians 1:15-17 he explains a different plan: he wanted to visit Corinth twice, on the way to and from Macedonia, and then did not, and his critics said he was fickle. Acts 20:1-3 records that he later went through Macedonia and spent three months in Greece.

p: 'Send me on my way' in Greek means to supply food, money and company for the next stage.
b: Propempō means more than waving goodbye. It means helping a traveler with supplies, money, guides and companions, as Paul hoped the church in Rome would do on his way to Spain (Romans 15:24) and as Titus is told to do for Zenas and Apollos (Titus 3:13). The Philippians' gifts to Paul (Philippians 4:14-18) were help of the same kind. Paul asks the Corinthians for this service, which is a mild way of reminding them of their part in his mission. "Wherever I may go" leaves his later plans open: Jerusalem (16:3-4), then Rome and Spain (Romans 15:24-28). Winter was a hard time for sea travel, so a stay in Corinth over the winter would also have made practical sense.

a: I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost
p: Paul writes from Ephesus before Pentecost; this fixes the place and the season of the letter.
b: Pentecost, the Jewish Feast of Weeks, fell fifty days after Passover (Leviticus 23:15-16), around late spring. "Until Pentecost" puts the writing before that feast, so in a spring. Acts says he stayed at Ephesus about two years and three months in all (Acts 19:8-10), and that he finally left after the riot (Acts 20:1). The letter was written about halfway through that stay. The later note at the end of the Textus Receptus saying it was written "from Philippi" contradicts this verse and is a scribal addition (see the variant note at 16:24).

a: a door has opened to me
t: An open door and many opponents
p: Paul sees open opportunity and strong opposition in the same city.
b: "A door opened" is Paul's image for a chance to preach (2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3; Acts 14:27). The Ephesus ministry had real results, as Acts 19:10 says: "everyone living in Asia heard the Lord's word, Jews and Greeks alike." The "opponents" were also real: the riot started by the silversmiths who made shrines to Artemis (Acts 19:23-41). Paul does not treat opposition as a sign to leave. He treats it as a reason to stay. The word "productive" (energēs) means "at work" or "effective," the root of our "energy."
orig: θύρα ... μεγάλη καὶ ἐνεργής (thyra ... megalē kai energēs)

p: Timothy is on his way, but the 'if' shows he may arrive after this letter.
b: Paul had written earlier that he was sending Timothy (4:17). Acts 19:22 says Paul sent Timothy and Erastus ahead into Macedonia, so Timothy may have been traveling the land route. The Greek ean elthē ("if he comes") allows that the letter might arrive first. Paul asks that Timothy have "nothing to fear" and that no one "treat him with contempt," because Timothy was young and reserved (compare 1 Timothy 4:12) and the Corinthians were quick to judge a speaker by his bearing (2 Corinthians 10:10). The phrase "as I am too" lifts Timothy to Paul's own rank in the Lord's work.

t: Whose will was it, Apollos's or God's?
p: The Greek says 'it was not at all will' and does not say whose; ancient readers differed.
b: The Greek reads "it was not at all thelēma (will, wish) that he should now come." The sentence leaves the owner of the will out. (1) Apollos's own wish: he did not want to go. Some think he stayed away so as not to feed the quarrels over "I belong to Apollos" (1:12). (2) God's will: some saw a divine hindrance. (3) Paul's will: Paul did not want him to go now, a reading few favor. Paul, who could command, only "urged," treating Apollos as a free colleague. The Plain English Translation's "his wish" follows the first reading and flags the others.

p: The Greek word means 'be brave'; it comes from the word for man but was used of women too.
b: Andrizesthe comes from anēr, "man," and earlier English versions say "quit you like men." It is a call to courage and appears in the Septuagint addressed to the whole people (Psalm 31:24 in the Plain English Translation: "Stay strong; let your hearts stand firm"; the Greek of that psalm has the verb). It occurs only here in the New Testament. Because the exhortation sits in a letter that gave women speaking roles in worship (11:5), it is best read as "be brave," a call to the whole church. The four short commands in a row sound like a military order, and the next verse turns them to love.

t: Stephanas and the first believers in Achaia
p: Stephanas's household were first converts in the province; Acts names others at Athens.
b: Achaia is the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital and Athens inside it. Paul says he baptized the household of Stephanas (1:16), and here calls them "the firstfruits of Achaia." Acts 17:34 reports that a few Athenians believed, among them Dionysius and Damaris, which seems to come earlier. Explanations: the Athenian converts did not form a household or a lasting church; or "firstfruits" means the first family of Corinth; or Paul uses the phrase loosely. The same word describes Epaenetus, "the firstfruits of Asia" (Romans 16:5).

a: put yourselves, too, under people like these
t: Submission to workers, not to office
p: The 'submission' is to those who labor in the work, a respect earned by service.
b: Hypotassesthe ("put yourselves under") is the verb for submitting, here a form that can be read as middle or as passive. The middle ("put yourselves under") makes it an act of choice, which is how the Plain English Translation reads it, but the form itself does not settle this. Paul names those who earn this standing by being sunergountes ("joining in the work") and kopiōntes ("laboring"), not by title or wealth. In a patronage society where rich householders expected honor, Stephanas's household gets it for service. The Corinthian leaders were chosen by other standards (1:26-29). Churches have applied the verse to respect for their ministers and elders. The text itself only says: honor those who work.

p: Three men came to Paul in Ephesus; they may have brought the Corinthians' letter.
b: Stephanas is Greek, Fortunatus is a Latin name ("lucky"), and Achaicus means "man of Achaia." The names suggest freed slaves or dependents of a household. They came to Ephesus and "filled up" what the church lacked, either the church's absence or the church's support for Paul. Many scholars think they brought the Corinthians' letter to Paul (7:1) and carried Paul's answer home. Chloe's people (1:11) were another channel of news. The Corinthians' contacts with Paul came through ordinary people who are named, which is typical of how Paul's churches stayed joined.

p: The couple Paul met in Corinth now live in Ephesus and host a church.
b: Acts 18:2 tells how Aquila and Priscilla, Jews expelled from Rome by Claudius, met Paul in Corinth; they sailed with him as far as Ephesus (Acts 18:18) and taught Apollos there (Acts 18:26). "Prisca" is the shorter form of "Priscilla"; Paul always uses it. They are in Ephesus when Paul writes and will be back in Rome by the time he writes Romans 16:3-5. Paul places Aquila first here and Prisca first in Romans 16:3; some read the order as a sign of her importance. They are the best example in the New Testament of a couple who served together in the church's work.

a: the church that meets in their house
p: A church often met in a large home; Paul names several such houses.
b: Early Christians had no church buildings. They met in homes, especially those of wealthier members whose dining room could hold thirty to fifty people. Romans 16:5 uses almost the same phrase: "Greet also the church that meets in their house." Other house churches: Nympha's (Colossians 4:15), Philemon's (Philemon 2), Gaius's at Corinth (Romans 16:23). Corinth's church seems to have met in several households (1:16; 16:15), which may explain part of the factions: each house had its own leader. A "church" in Paul's sense is the gathering, not the building.

p: A greeting kiss among believers, set apart as 'holy'; it became part of early worship.
b: Greeting a relative or friend with a kiss was normal in the ancient Mediterranean. Paul asks that it be "holy": a sign of family love among believers of different classes and backgrounds. He repeats the instruction in 2 Corinthians 13:12, Romans 16:16 and 1 Thessalonians 5:26, and 1 Peter 5:14 has the "kiss of love." By the 100s it was part of the Eucharist: Justin Martyr says the believers greet each other with a kiss before the bread and wine are brought (First Apology 65). The Catholic, Orthodox and some Protestant liturgies keep it as the "sign of peace."

p: Paul dictated letters to a scribe and signed the end in his own writing.
b: Most of Paul's letters were written down by a secretary, as Tertius says of Romans (Romans 16:22). At the end, Paul took the pen himself to add a line that proved the letter was his. Galatians 6:11 and Colossians 4:18 do the same, and 2 Thessalonians 3:17 calls it his mark in every letter. The scribe of 1 Corinthians is not named, though Sosthenes is a co-sender (1:1). The words "in my own hand" explain the shift in tone in the last lines: the personal warning (16:22) and the offer of love (16:24) are the apostle's own voice.

p: Paul uses phileo, 'to be a friend to', here only in his undisputed letters.
b: Almost everywhere Paul writes agapaō for love. Here alone in his undisputed letters he writes phileō, the word for personal affection and loyalty, such as friends and family share. The site's term entry says both are rendered "love" and the note names the Greek where it matters. Here the curse is aimed at someone who lacks personal loyalty to the Lord, not at someone who fails to understand a doctrine. It reads as a test of loyalty: those who belong to the Lord are in, and those who do not are out. Compare John 21:15-17, where Jesus uses both verbs.

a: that person is to be accursed
p: Anathema first meant something set apart for God; in Paul it is a curse or a ban.
b: Anathema is a thing set apart for God, which in Jewish and Christian use became a thing given over to destruction, and so a curse (Deuteronomy 7:26 in the Septuagint). Paul uses it in Galatians 1:8-9 against a different gospel, in Romans 9:3 of himself (if he could be cut off for Israel), and in 1 Corinthians 12:3 against anyone who says "Jesus is accursed." The grammar is a third-person command, ētō anathema: "let him be a curse." Whether it is a ban from the community, a handing over to God's judgment, or a warning is debated. The churches later used "anathema" for formal exclusion; see the card on church discipline at chapter 5.

t: 'Our Lord, come' or 'Our Lord has come'
p: An Aramaic prayer of the first Jerusalem church, left untranslated in a Greek letter.
b: Marana tha is Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, which Greek-speaking Corinth would not have known unless it was a catchword of the faith. The words can be divided two ways. Maranā thā: "Our Lord, come!" (imperative, a prayer). Maran atā: "Our Lord has come" (perfect), or "is coming" (a statement). Revelation 22:20 translates the prayer: "Come, Lord Jesus!" and the Didache (10:6) uses it at the end of the Lord's Supper prayers. Most scholars take it as a prayer. It shows that the Aramaic-speaking believers called Jesus Mar, "Lord," and prayed to him (Larry Hurtado).

a: My love goes with all of you
t: Paul ends with love, not just grace
p: No other Pauline letter ends with Paul's own love; it follows a letter with hard words.
b: Paul's usual last words are "grace," as in verse 23. Only here does he add "my love." After hard words about factions, lawsuits, idol meat, the Lord's Supper and the doubters of the resurrection, he closes by telling them he loves them all, including those he has corrected. "All of you" includes the party members, the proud and the wronged. The additional "Amen" and the longer ending that says the letter was "written from Philippi through Stephanas, Fortunatus, Achaicus and Timothy" appear only in later manuscripts (the Textus Receptus); it does not agree with 16:8, which puts Paul in Ephesus.
